item.title: How Harsh Vardhan Goenka became founding engineer #1 at Kalpa Labs
item.description: From ICPC World Finals to competitive programming clubs to building generalist audio models as the first engineer at a YC startup.
item.dc:creator: Frank Stratton
item.content:encoded:
Before Harsh Vardhan Goenka joined Kalpa Labs, he was at Rubrik Inc., where he helped build Rubrik Cloud Vault from its early days and rewrote the company's testing infrastructure so that test suites that took hours ran in minutes. He'd always gravitated toward small teams and hard problems — competitive programming took him to the ICPC World Finals, and engineering at scale brought him to Rubrik. But the pull toward something smaller, scrappier, and more frontier kept growing. When his former college seniors founded Kalpa Labs (YC F25), a company building generalist audio models, the timing finally clicked.

An 11 PM interview on a spare Windows laptop

item.title: How Dylan Anderson became founding engineer at Adam
item.description: Dylan left Minnesota for San Francisco to build AI agents for CAD software as the first engineer at Adam (W25).
item.dc:creator: Frank Stratton
item.content:encoded:
Dylan Anderson was a software engineer at, in his words, "some random place in Minnesota." Then a friend-of-a-friend connection changed everything. A roommate of Adam's founders was asked if he knew any cracked engineers. Dylan's name came up. He did a work trial, moved to San Francisco, and became the first engineer at Adam (W25), a company building AI agents for CAD software.

Why he said yes

item.title: How Andrew HunzekerHesed became Employee #1 at 10x Science
item.description: A principal engineer left consumer-scale software to build AI-native scientific analysis tools as the founding engineer at 10x Science.
item.dc:creator: Frank Stratton
item.content:encoded: Andrew HunzekerHesed spent years building software seen by millions of people — food delivery logistics, CPG stocking at Walmart, video streaming at Major League Baseball, and most recently serving as Principal Engineer at Grindr. The work was fun and visible, but the general software development lifecycle was starting to look the same everywhere: "Exec to Design to PM to Engineer, with ever-increasing velocity due to AI." Then he met the founders of 10x Science (W26) at a talent summit, and something shifted.

item.title: How Max Friedlander became founding operations at Petrarch
item.description: A math major who turned down safe internships to lead high-stakes deals at a YC S26 startup supplying data for frontier AI labs.
item.dc:creator: Frank Stratton
item.content:encoded:
Max Friedlander was building voice agents for service businesses when a LinkedIn message changed his trajectory. Ian, one of the founders of Petrarch, reached out to pick his brain about voice AI data. Max told them the idea wouldn't work. They kept talking anyway. When the team mentioned they had a YC interview coming up, Max asked them to keep him posted. A few weeks later, they got in — and a couple days after that, they asked if he wanted to be an intern. "Just based on the vibes from the call we had before," Max says.

He was employee number five. He's 20 years old, an applied mathematics major at Middlebury College, and he does sales at Petrarch, a YC S26 company that supplies data for frontier AI labs.

Why he said yes

item.title: How David Mount became employee #2 (for the second time) at 10x Science
item.description: A veteran engineer finds his next act helping scientists discover cures, one amino acid at a time, at YC W26 startup 10x Science.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded:
David Mount has started four companies, served as CTO, watched funding dry up, and built a passion project about nuclear energy called Atomic Ambitions. When his previous startup, Chinchill.AI, ran out of money, he signed up on YC's Work at a Startup. Two weeks later, a founder from 10x Science reached out — someone who had actually taken the time to experience Atomic Ambitions. That detail mattered.

10x Science (W26) uses AI to process scientific data and unlock bio-chemical discovery, with work already proven in cellular-scale advances across medicine, biotech, and pharmacology.

A work trial that felt like a final exam

item.title: How Yair Alon went from building Portrait Mode at Google to founding researcher at Poetiq
item.description: After 10 years at Google Research and DeepMind, Yair Alon joined Poetiq to build an AI that improves itself.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded:
Yair Alon spent a decade at Google Research and DeepMind. He built the deep learning models behind Portrait Mode on Pixel phones. He published papers on efficient deep learning. He designed models for Search, Ads, and YouTube. His last project was VideoPoet, a video generation system. Everything was great, by his own account. But he felt that small startups had become where the most exciting innovations were happening. So when former DeepMind collaborators told him they were starting a company, he knew immediately he wanted in.

That company is Poetiq (YC S26, San Francisco). In one sentence: Poetiq is building an AI system that can optimize any other AI system, including itself.

Leaving Google after a decade

item.title: How Varsha Parthasarathy became engineer #1 at Flex — solving a problem she'd experienced
item.description: From Lyft's self-driving division to fixing HSA/FSA payments, Varsha joined Flex as its first engineer and built from scratch.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded:
When Varsha Parthasarathy was pregnant, she needed a letter from her doctor's office just to use her own HSA money on pregnancy-related expenses. Everything was already in her chart. She still had to send her husband or her sibling to the admin office to chase down the paperwork. Four months after her first kid was born, running on very little sleep and definitely not planning a career move, she sat down with her former Lyft colleague Miguel — one of the cofounders of Flex (S23) — to work together for a week in San Francisco. By the end of that week, she was in.

Flex helps businesses accept HSA and FSA payments, so people can use their pre-tax health dollars on products and services they're already buying. It plugs into a merchant's existing checkout and shows up as another way to pay, like Klarna or Google Pay.

item.title: How Sherif Amer went from electronics engineer to employee #1 at Indemni
item.description: A layoff, two years of travel, and a self-taught pivot to software led Sherif Amer to become the founding engineer at Indemni.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded:
Before he ever wrote a line of code for a startup, Sherif Amer was designing embedded systems and verifying mixed-signal chips at Infineon. Then an unexpected layoff changed his trajectory. Rather than jumping back into semiconductors, he spent two and a half years traveling the world, teaching himself software engineering, and building his own product — a project called Roamies. That winding path eventually brought him to Indemni (W24), a San Francisco startup that combines driver verification, carrier intelligence, and real-time shipment monitoring to help freight brokers detect fraud and move loads with confidence. Sherif was employee #1.

From hardware to founding engineer

item.title: How Alex Lee became the first engineer at Magic Patterns
item.description: Alex Lee left his own startup to join Magic Patterns as founding engineer — and built a slide deck feature in a weekend.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded: Before Alex Lee joined Magic Patterns (W23), he was running his own company, Iago — one that's still self-running today. But when his former Robinhood colleague Teddy co-founded Magic Patterns, a tool that helps product designers create interactive mockups and prototypes, Alex saw something he couldn't pass up: an AI-first approach to a problem he'd hit himself while building new features at Iago. "It's pretty clear that Figma is going to be replaced and a company like Magic Patterns is here to replace it," he says.

item.title: How Vin Bui became engineer #1 at Nowadays — and started treating it like his own company
item.description: Vin found Nowadays on Work at a Startup, saw a codebase he could fix, and joined as the first engineer. Now he builds AI voice tools and mentors the team.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Choi
item.content:encoded:
Vin Bui was on a leave of absence from Cornell when he found Nowadays. He had just left his own YC company from the Winter 2025 batch and was back on campus, not enrolled, scrolling through Work at a Startup looking for what came next. A dog logo caught his eye. "It felt childlike in a way, and that unique taste is what originally attracted me," he says. Then he looked at the website. "This website needed a lot more work. I really like seeing companies that have things I know I could fix."

He sent a message to co-founder Anna, went through the interview process, and became the first full-time hire at Nowadays (S23), a San Francisco company that uses AI to make planning corporate events simple. When it started, Nowadays was selling to small startups. Today it’s the platform Fortune 500 companies like Google, Airbnb, and BlackRock use to bring their people together.
